children.text: Before an application ever reaches an admissions committee, it goes through one more read that most families never think to ask for. Join Denard, a former admissions officer at Elon College, for a behind-the-scenes look at what an admissions committee review actually catches—the inconsistencies, missed opportunities, and small mistakes that quietly cost strong applicants. You'll see what a real AdCom-style review looks like in practice, evaluated the same way a college's own committee would read it. Ben will walk through why a student's own perspective on their file is often the least reliable one, and what it means to have a former admissions officer catch a problem before submission instead of after. If your student is finishing applications this fall, this is the review that happens before it's too late to fix anything.
In this webinar, you'll learn:
What a Committee Actually Catches:
Inconsistencies between an essay, an activity description, and a recommendation letter are invisible to a student — but not to a trained reader.
Read the Way It Will Be Read:
An AdCom review evaluates a file the same way a real admissions committee does, before submission instead of after.
The Last Chance to Fix It:
Once an application is submitted, there's no second read. This is the review that happens while changes are still possible.

items.title: What It Really Takes to Get Into the Ivy League
items.teaser: Every Ivy League applicant pool is full of 4.0s, perfect scores, and long activity lists — which means none of that actually separates the admits. Former Brown admissions officer Daniel breaks down what a reader is really scoring once academic qualification is a given, and why a coherent story across activities and essays becomes the true differentiator. This isn't a list of hacks — it's the framework Daniel used to evaluate thousands of files.

children.text: Every Ivy League applicant pool is full of 4.0s, perfect scores, and long activity lists, which means none of that is actually what separates the admits. Join Daniel, a former Brown admissions officer, for a direct look at what a reader is actually scoring once academic qualification is a given. He'll break down why "well-rounded" is often the wrong goal, what makes an essay memorable instead of forgettable at eleven at night on file four hundred, and how a coherent story across activities and essays becomes the real differentiator. This isn't a list of hacks—it's the framework Daniel used to evaluate thousands of files. Bring your questions for live Q&A at the end.
In this webinar, you'll learn:
Qualified Is the Floor:
Nearly every Ivy applicant is academically qualified. Daniel explains what actually happens once that's no longer the question.
One Person, Not a Resume:
Readers assemble a portrait from the file, not a checklist. Learn what makes activities and essays read as one coherent person.
The Sentence a Reader Needs:
A reader has to describe your student in one sentence to a committee. Daniel shows you how to give them that sentence — or force them to invent a worse one.

children.text: Daniel M. brings five years of experience in undergraduate admissions to Empowerly. Most recently, he served as a Senior Admissions Officer at Brown University. Before his time at Brown, Daniel was an Assistant Director of Admissions at Connecticut College, where he earned his B.A. in Economics. Over the past five years, Daniel has reviewed over 5,000 college applications, interviewed hundreds of prospective students, and played a key role in more than 50 admission committees. He has evaluated applicants from across the country, representing a variety of school systems and academic interests, including Computer Science, Engineering, the Humanities, Social Sciences, and the Visual Arts.

Additionally, Daniel has made decisions on students applying to Brown’s BS/MD program (PLME), recruited athletes, and those pursuing the Brown/RISD dual degree program. Throughout his time in admissions, Daniel has had one-on-one conversations with prospective students about building competitive application profiles. He’s also volunteered as a college counselor, where he’s reviewed essays, helped students build college lists, and educated students on standardized testing. What excites him the most about college counseling is the chance to build genuine relationships with students and serve as a supportive guide during this pivotal time in their lives.

items.title: How to Get Into a BS/MD Program
items.teaser: Direct medical programs admit a class the size of a large lecture hall from a pool in the thousands — and every applicant already has the grades, scores, and hospital hours. Former Brown PLME admissions officer Daniel breaks down what actually separates admitted students from an otherwise identical, rejected pool, and why the real work starts in 9th and 10th grade, not senior fall. If your student is serious about medicine, replace guesswork with the exact framework a reader uses to decide.

children.text: Direct medical programs admit a class the size of a large lecture hall from a pool in the thousands — and every applicant already has the grades, the scores, and the hospital hours. Join Daniel, a former senior admissions officer for Brown's PLME program, where he'll break down what actually separates admitted students from an otherwise identical, rejected pool. You'll learn why committees read BS/MD applications as a commitment they're underwriting eight years early and what that means for how your student should be spending 9th and 10th grade, not just senior fall. Daniel will walk through real examples of what makes an essay, a research line, or a clinical hour actually count versus quietly blend in. If your student is serious about medicine, this session replaces guesswork with the exact framework a reader uses to decide.
In this webinar, you'll learn:
Shortcut vs. Commitment:
Families see BS/MD as a faster path. Committees see a bet on a teenager's certainty — and read every line of the file to test it.
Evidence Takes Years, Not a Summer:
Clinical hours, research, and leadership all take two to three years to build real depth. Senior fall can only describe what already exists.
One Sentence, One Committee:
A reader isn't scoring your essay — they're deciding if they can describe your student in one sentence tomorrow morning. Learn how to give them that sentence.
